item.title: APEC Primer in Four Words | Together: Three priorities shaping APEC 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
APEC Primer in Four Words | Together: Three priorities shaping APEC 2026 This photo taken on Nov. 3, 2026 shows an APEC-themed installation at a park in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian) APEC Primer in Four Words: The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." This four-part series unpacks four key words from that theme, one each day, to explain what APEC is and what the 2026 host year is about. Trade, technology and economic resilience present different challenges for the Asia-Pacific. But they have something in common: progress often depends on economies working beyond their own borders. "Together," the final word of the theme, is where the year's work comes into focus. Across China's host year, APEC's 21 economies have pursued three priorities: openness, innovation and cooperation. In practice, that has meant making cross-border trade easier, responding to the rise of artificial intelligence and building economic resilience. Openness: trade and connectivity On trade, policy dialogues this year have covered trade digitalization, competition policy, state-owned enterprises, and trade and labor, as part of discussions toward the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP). There has also been progress on paperless trade. APEC has established a Center of Excellence for Paperless Trade and is working to improve how electronic trade systems communicate across borders. APEC research suggests that digitalizing trade documents could cut trade transaction costs by 5.8 percent. Connectivity is being revisited too. China has called for an upgrade to the APEC Connectivity Blueprint for 2015 to 2025, which was endorsed at the 2014 Beijing meeting, to make physical, institutional and people-to-people links more effective. Innovation: digital, smart and green Wang Yi, China's minister of foreign affairs, has called for digital, smart and green transformations driven by innovation, as well as people-centered artificial intelligence (AI) and "AI for good." Throughout the year, APEC economies have examined how different approaches to AI governance can work together, including on data privacy, trust and technical standards. They have also looked at AI applications in energy, services and trade, alongside digital literacy and workforce development. AI is expected to feature prominently when leaders meet in Shenzhen. Readiness is a recurring theme. Carlos Kuriyama, director of the APEC Policy Support Unit, said the benefits of AI are going mainly to economies that are ready to embrace it, which is why digital readiness and capacity building are part of the agenda. Cooperation: shared goals The third priority is about what economies can achieve together beyond trade and technology. Ministerial meetings this year have produced outcomes on digital infrastructure financing, financial inclusion, energy systems and food systems resilience. These issues cross national and economic boundaries. Disruptions to energy supplies and food systems can affect economies across the region, while access to financing and infrastructure shapes their ability to respond. Cooperation offers opportunities to share experience, coordinate approaches and strengthen resilience. APEC Secretariat Executive Director Eduardo Pedrosa has described the forum as a place where economies share experiences, compare policy approaches and identify where further progress can be made. The regional economy provides a backdrop for those discussions. According to APEC's Policy Support Unit, the region is projected to grow 3.4 percent in 2026, up from 3.2 percent in 2025. Sustaining that growth while addressing shared vulnerabilities remains an important challenge. Four words, one theme APEC Economic Leaders' Week began Nov. 14 with meetings of senior officials and business representatives, ahead of the Economic Leaders' Meeting on Nov. 18 and 19. Taken together, the four words in this series describe one idea. "Community" is the relationship among 21 economies, and "Prosper" is their shared ambition. "Building" is the sustained work needed to realize it, with Shenzhen's transformation as one example. "Together" is how they try to do it. Building an Asia-Pacific community is not the work of a single meeting or host year. The measure of success will be what the region's economies can continue to achieve together. item.title: From Beijing to Shenzhen: China's push for a more connected, dynamic Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
From Beijing to Shenzhen: China's push for a more connected, dynamic Asia-Pacific BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China, from Nov. 18 to 19, marking the first time in 12 years that China is hosting the APEC meeting, following Beijing in 2014. The Beijing meeting endorsed a vision of an integrated, innovative, and interconnected Asia-Pacific, calling for closer links in infrastructure, trade, and people-to-people exchanges. Over the past 12 years, China has worked with other APEC economies to advance that vision, expanding cooperation from transport and trade facilitation to digital and green development. This year's gathering, to be held under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," will focus on three priority areas identified by China -- openness, innovation, and cooperation -- and is expected to help regional economies deepen economic ties and foster new drivers of growth. People walk past an APEC-themed installation at Gangxia North Metro Station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian) ADVANCING CONNECTIVITY At Yantian Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, nearly 100 international shipping routes operate each week, 53 of them connecting the port with other APEC economies. The flow of goods through the port reflects the growing connectivity and deepening economic ties between China and the wider region. Connectivity was a priority of China's 2014 APEC host year. At the Beijing meeting, leaders and representatives endorsed China's proposal to establish the APEC Cooperation Network on Green Supply Chain and approved the establishment of its first pilot center in north China's Tianjin. The center officially opened in June 2015 to promote green procurement and supply-chain assessment. The Green Supply Chain Network has grown into a key platform for regional cooperation on green trade. Trade agreements have also translated integration into business opportunities. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), which came into force in 2022, has provided a foundation for deeper cooperation toward prosperity, resilience, and sustainability. RCEP binds ASEAN's 10 members at that time with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand into the largest free trade zone in the world by population and GDP share. By lowering tariffs and harmonizing trade rules, RCEP is estimated to further boost intra-regional trade significantly and strengthen integrated regional supply chains. Alongside RCEP, the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (CAFTA) has been significantly upgraded under CAFTA 3.0, which was signed at the 28th ASEAN-China Summit in October 2025. The new version expands the traditional trade pact far beyond tariff reduction. With nine new areas covering the digital economy, green economy and supply chain connectivity, among others, CAFTA 3.0 marks a milestone in economic cooperation that strengthens collective resilience amid global uncertainty. An aerial drone photo taken on April 13, 2026 shows a train of the China-Laos Railway, departing from Kunming of southwest China's Yunnan Province, arriving in Vientiane, Laos. (Photo by Xia Ningqin/Xinhua) China has also actively promoted infrastructure in the region. Jointly built and operated by China and Laos, the China-Laos Railway links Kunming in southwest China's Yunnan Province with the Lao capital Vientiane, providing landlocked Laos with a rail link to China and access to wider regional markets. Since operation in December 2021, it has carried more than 20.77 million tonnes of import and export goods worth over 100.4 billion yuan (about 15 billion U.S. dollars). The flow goes both ways: durians, mangosteens and other tropical fruits travel north, while Chinese machinery and electronics move south, bringing producers and markets across the region closer together. FOSTERING NEW GROWTH As regional connections have expanded, cooperation has moved beyond trade to encompass technologies and industries that will help shape future growth. At the 2014 Beijing meeting, APEC leaders and representatives endorsed the Accord on Innovative Development, Economic Reform and Growth, highlighting innovation and economic reform as drivers of regional growth. Trade data point to the growing importance of technology in regional economic ties. In 2025, China's high-tech exports to other APEC economies rose 8.1 percent to 4.63 trillion yuan (about 694 billion dollars), according to the General Administration of Customs. Shenzhen's growing AI sector offers a glimpse of the technological capabilities China can bring to regional cooperation. By the end of 2025, the city had more than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size, with core AI industry revenue of about 220 billion yuan (about 32.97 billion dollars). At APEC business and AI forums in June 2026, participants from 13 APEC economies discussed AI applications and cross-border cooperation, while institutions from China, South Korea, Indonesia and other economies signed agreements on technology commercialization and cross-border industrial parks. This photo taken on July 4, 2026 shows an embodied intelligence robot displayed at AIR Design House in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) Antonio Basilio, director of the APEC Business Advisory Council Secretariat, said China's experience demonstrated the importance of translating technological innovation into practical economic applications, particularly in manufacturing, logistics, agriculture and services. These technological advances are also reflected in Shenzhen's export mix. In 2025, electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, photovoltaic products, AI-powered products, and medical instruments and equipment together accounted for 25.6 percent of Shenzhen's exports to other APEC economies. Chinese technology and investment are contributing to industrial development across the region. In Malaysia, Chinese battery maker EVE Energy has brought the second phase of its lithium battery plant into operation, the Southeast Asian country's first such large-scale factory. Located in northwestern Malaysia, the facility has an annual production capacity of 680 million cylindrical battery cells. In Thailand, BYD's Rayong plant has an annual production capacity of 150,000 vehicles and employs more than 6,000 people, about 95 percent of them Thai nationals. Mackenzie Lang, CEO of the Australia-China Youth Group, described Shenzhen as "a city everybody across the world now associates with technological innovation and economic development." He expressed hope that this year's APEC meeting would foster stronger regional economic ties and investment. SHARING PROSPERITY China's expanding market offers companies from other APEC economies opportunities to reach Chinese consumers and build lasting partnerships, while providing regional partners with much-needed expertise and capital. Shenzhen's growing economic ties with the region are a snapshot of this broader cooperation. In the first half of 2026, the city's trade with other APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan (about 296.8 billion dollars), up 33 percent year on year, while investment by local enterprises in other APEC members accounted for nearly 60 percent of Shenzhen's total outbound investment. Meanwhile, the China International Import Expo (CIIE), now in its ninth edition, has also provided a platform for companies from other APEC economies to enter the Chinese market. This photo taken on Nov. 10, 2026 shows the exhibition area of Intelligent Industry and Information Technology of the 9th China International Import Expo in east China's Shanghai. (Xinhua/Han Xiaoyu) Australian dairy producer Bulla, which has participated in the expo every year since 2019, reached a direct-sourcing agreement with Chinese grocery platform Dingdong Fresh at the 2025 CIIE. Sam Zhang, who oversees international business at Bulla, said the company's exports to China exceeded 10 million Australian dollars (about 7 million dollars) in the financial year ended June 30, 2026. Beyond expanding market access, China has also worked with other APEC economies to promote development cooperation that benefits local communities. In Papua New Guinea, nearly three decades of cooperation with China on Juncao (the herbal plant for growing edible mushrooms) technology have created new income opportunities for rural households. First introduced to the country's Eastern Highlands Province in 1997, the technology has since been promoted through demonstration centers and farmer training programs. With guidance from Chinese agricultural experts, local farmer Zaka Abori began cultivating edible mushrooms in February 2020. China's International Development Cooperation Agency reported in 2022 that she earned an annual income of 15,000 kina (about 4,240 dollars) from mushroom cultivation, about seven times the annual income of most families in the area engaged in coffee and vegetable farming. By March 2025, Juncao and upland rice technologies had been promoted in 20 districts across 10 provinces of Papua New Guinea, with 3,277 people trained. In April 2026, Prime Minister James Marape called for a major expansion of the partnership, citing its contributions to rural livelihoods and agricultural development. Hans Hendrischke, professor of Chinese business and management at the University of Sydney Business School, said APEC's priorities of openness, innovation and cooperation address fundamental challenges facing the Asia-Pacific region, from resisting protectionism and embracing new technologies to developing common rules for cooperation. Shenzhen summit first face-to-face meeting among Chinese, Russian, U.S. heads of state in history: spokesperson (Xinhua) 16:28, November 16, 2026 BEIJING, Nov. 16 (Xinhua) -- The meeting of Chinese, Russian, U.S. heads of state in China's Shenzhen will be the first face-to-face meeting among the top leaders of the three countries in history, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Monday. Mao made the remarks when asked to answer a related query, saying that the heads of state will have an in-depth exchange of views on maintaining world peace and promoting strategic stability in major country relations. Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold a China-Russia-U.S. summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson announced on Monday morning. item.title: Together for a bright Asia-Pacific future
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Together for a bright Asia-Pacific future The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong province, on Nov. 18 and 19. As the host economy making its third appearance at the table, China will work with other member economies to chart a blueprint for Asia-Pacific cooperation, focusing on three priorities: openness, innovation, and cooperation. Together, they will advance the building of an open, dynamic, resilient, and peaceful Asia-Pacific community, injecting fresh impetus into peace and development in the region and beyond. At the first APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in 1993, a landmark decision was made to move beyond the outdated mentality of bloc confrontation and zero-sum games, deepen economic cooperation and integration in the region, and build a dynamic, harmonious, and prosperous Asia-Pacific community. Established amid the wave of economic globalization, APEC aims to promote trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, as well as support economic growth and prosperity. It has helped keep the Asia-Pacific at the forefront of global openness and development. Home to about 40 percent of the world's population, the Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60 percent of global GDP and nearly half of world trade, making it a major engine of global economic growth, an anchor of stability for global development, and a hub of cooperation. In 2020, APEC adopted the Putrajaya Vision 2040, reaffirming its founding mission to improve living standards across the region. The roadmap sets a clear target: to realize an open, dynamic, resilient, and peaceful Asia-Pacific community by 2040. 2026 marks another APEC "China Year." Under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," member economies are advancing broader consensus on the community's institutional architecture and laying the groundwork for its long-term operational framework. Sustainable regional progress hinges on enhanced connectivity. Greater openness and seamless cross-border linkages enable Asia-Pacific economies to overcome market fragmentation, deepen cooperative ties, and unlock new avenues for growth. The APEC Connectivity Blueprint for 2015-2025, adopted in Beijing in 2014, mapped out a path toward a comprehensive, multi-tiered, and multidimensional Asia-Pacific connectivity network. This year, drawing on the final review of the 10-year blueprint, member economies are developing an upgraded version. Shenzhen, the host city of this year's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, is a vibrant city known for its openness and innovation. Where does the vitality of the Asia-Pacific come from? China's answer is innovation. The Asia-Pacific boasts unique intellectual resources and a well-established tradition of innovation. It has given rise to numerous new technologies, industries, and mechanisms, and has long been at the global forefront of innovation. According to the 2026 rankings released by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster ranked first among the world's innovation clusters for the second consecutive year. It was followed by the Tokyo-Yokohama cluster, the San Jose-San Francisco cluster, Seoul, Beijing, and the Shanghai-Suzhou cluster. The rankings underscore the Asia-Pacific's weight in the global innovation landscape. In 2014, APEC economic leaders endorsed the APEC Accord on Innovative Development, Economic Reform and Growth, charting a course for innovative development in the region. In 2026, member economies are deepening practical cooperation in digital transformation and artificial intelligence, generating fresh momentum for a dynamic Asia-Pacific community. Can resilience be maintained amid growing uncertainty? In October, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its Regional Economic Outlook: Asia and Pacific, highlighted three major factors shaping the region's economic outlook: the energy shock arising from conflicts in the Middle East, the AI-driven technology boom, and continued trade reconfiguration. True resilience extends beyond shock absorption and short-term stability; it requires the capacity to foster long-term, sustainable development. China advocates for universally beneficial, inclusive, green, and sustainable development. This approach, which strengthens the foundations for growth and is future-oriented, reveals what fuels development resilience and how to sustain it. The Asia-Pacific has suffered from conflicts and wars in the past. It was only after emerging from the shadow of the Cold War that the region, particularly its small- and medium-sized economies, embarked on a fast track toward modernization and created "the Asia-Pacific miracle." Building a peaceful Asia-Pacific community requires drawing wisdom from history, staying on course. Peace and development reinforce each other and must be advanced together. Peace does not come automatically; it must be actively built. Peace cannot be secured once and for all; it must be carefully safeguarded. Asia-Pacific economies should jointly uphold peaceful development and win-win cooperation, and work together to implement the four major global initiatives. Only by doing so can they continue to build up collective strength to safeguard peace and stability in the region. The official emblem for APEC China 2026 features 21 interlaced feathers arranged to form the silhouette of the Peng, a mythical creature from Chinese legend that transforms from a giant fish into a soaring bird. The design symbolizes the 21 APEC member economies harnessing the momentum of regional collaboration to rise together. Setting fresh sail from Shenzhen, the vessel of Asia-Pacific cooperation will surge forward, charting a course toward the realization of an open, dynamic, resilient, and peaceful Asia-Pacific community. item.title: Xi congratulates Jinan University on its 120th founding anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Xi congratulates Jinan University on its 120th founding anniversary BEIJING, Nov. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Monday sent a congratulatory letter to Jinan University, celebrating its 120th founding anniversary. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, extended congratulations to the faculty, students and alumni of the university. Xi urged the university to carry forward its patriotic traditions and distinctive educational features, and to foster more young talent among compatriots in Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan and overseas Chinese. He also called on the university to carry forward and promote Chinese culture and advance friendly exchanges between China and the world. The university was asked to improve its education and teaching quality and make new contributions to pooling strength among overseas Chinese and advancing Chinese modernization. Founded in 1906, the university in south China's Guangdong Province has, over the past 120 years, nurtured a wealth of outstanding talent for Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, as well as for more than 170 countries. item.title: Shenzhen's innovation creates new opportunities for Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Shenzhen's innovation creates new opportunities for Asia-Pacific Over the past four decades, Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province has grown into an innovation hub — and in 2014 it became home to the country's first national independent innovation demonstration zone to cover an entire city. "Innovation capital" has become the city's signature label. Visitors watch a robot performance outside the world's first robot 6S store in Longgang district, Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 21. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) Shenzhen will host the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19. Under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," the meeting has identified openness, innovation and cooperation as its three priority areas. The economies should fully harness new technologies to empower and propel them forward, seize the opportunities of digital, smart and green development, and move faster to nurture and promote new quality productive forces, Chinese President Xi Jinping said at the second session of the 32nd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting held last year. Unmanned delivery vehicles made by autonomous vehicle company Neolix sets off to deliver goods after completing a subway shuttle trip at Futian subway station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Photo courtesy of the integrated media center of Longgang district) Shenzhen's innovation can be seen on the ground. Driverless delivery vehicles made by autonomous vehicle company Neolix, powered by a self-developed AI model and Level 4 autonomous driving technology, now handle cold-chain fresh food, retail and medicine delivery alongside express parcels. Chen Xuelin, head of the company's Shenzhen operations, told People's Daily Online that the fleet numbers more than 30,000 vehicles across more than 20 countries and regions, and has cut end-to-end logistics costs by 30 to 50 percent. These advances rest on a complete ecosystem for intelligent connected vehicles in Shenzhen, spanning legislation, uses, algorithms and manufacturing. In 2022, the city became the first in China to pass legislation governing such vehicles, making it a testing ground for new technologies and products. A researcher works at a shared laboratory platform for scientists and doctors provided by the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) In Guangming district, the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation and the Shenzhen Bay Laboratory have joined forces to build a biomedical innovation chain covering basic research, technological breakthroughs and clinical translation. Their shared public platforms have served hundreds of institutions and logged more than 30,000 user visits, helping bring down research and development costs. Nearby, Bay Charm, a biomedical incubator run jointly by the Guangming district government and the Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, has helped launch more than 40 companies in three years, said Wu Yulun, its operations manager. Photo shows a corner of the world's first AI 6S store in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Xu Xiangli) The robot block in Longgang district is home to two world firsts: an AI 6S store and a robot 6S store. Since the AI store opened in July 2025, it has drawn an average of more than 500 visitors a day, 30 percent of them from overseas. Foreign visits to the block have risen from 80,000 to 500,000 a year. Many foreign buyers now bring product ideas to Shenzhen to turn them into reality. An AI doll that can talk can go from concept to prototype in as little as 48 hours, at a cost of no more than 3,000 yuan (about $450). "Shenzhen is the first choice for anyone who wants to bring hardware products to market efficiently," said Huang Qiao, head of the AI store. Longgang's dense network of suppliers at every stage of production lets buyers source components, prototyping and manufacturing in one place. A robot works at X Square Robot Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) Platforms and mechanisms lay the groundwork, but what matters in the end is whether businesses themselves are thriving. That depends on technology, finance and talent working together. X Square Robot Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. released WALL-B, world's first embodied foundation model based on a World Unified Model architecture, in April. Its household service has been selected for APEC's Case Collection of Digital and AI Empowerment in Asia-Pacific Region at the High-level Dialogue: Leveraging Digital and AI Technologies to Empower the APEC Community. WeBank, a Shenzhen-based online bank, has served nearly 450 million individual customers and provided credit to more than 8.4 million micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Photo taken on Oct. 23, 2026 shows the office area of WeBank in Qianhai, Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) Shenzhen's total R&D spending reached 245 billion yuan (about $34 billion) in 2025, with R&D intensity at 6.67 percent, the highest among Chinese cities. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster ranked first in WIPO's Global Innovation Index. Huawei, ZTE, Tencent, BYD and DJI all grew out of Shenzhen's innovation ecosystem, one now supported by 128 proof-of-concept centers and pilot testing bases, and more than 4,000 innovation platforms at national, provincial and municipal levels. Shenzhen is exporting more than goods. Its service hall for SMEs expanding overseas brokers cooperation deals worth an average of more than 10 billion yuan (about $1.4 billion) a year. WeBank's technology arm has partnered with more than 35 institutions across Belt and Road partner countries — Indonesia, Thailand and the UAE among them — to upgrade their digital banking systems. And the Longgang Energy Eco-Park has taken its waste-to-energy technology to Southeast Asia and Kazakhstan. Employees at the Longgang Energy Eco-Park monitors real-time footage of each stage of waste incineration in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 21. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) Innovation is not only Shenzhen's hallmark but also a powerful engine for the Asia-Pacific region to overcome challenges. China stands ready to work with all parties to harness innovation and pave the way for win-win outcomes. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: 10 years on, world's first Luban Workshop helps create brighter future for Thai youth
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
10 years on, world's first Luban Workshop helps create brighter future for Thai youth Students practice the console for China's high-speed train CRH380B driving simulation system at the Luban Workshop in Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya Technical College in Ayutthaya, Thailand, Feb. 20, 2019. (Xinhua/Yang Zhou) AYUTTHAYA, Thailand, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- In a classroom at Ayutthaya Technical College, home to the world's first Luban Workshop jointly established by China and Thailand, several humanoid desktop robots rhythmically waved their arms and stepped to the music as Surapat Pimrat skillfully operated them. "I named one of the robots Nam Khing because it keeps me company like a best friend," said Surapat, a third-year student pursuing Vocational Certification in mechatronics and robotics at the workshop. He added that his sister, a workshop graduate now working at Haier Thailand, inspired him to enroll. Surapat's next plan is to pursue an opportunity to deepen his expertise in China, following his sister's example: she strengthened her professional expertise and improved her Chinese-language proficiency, paving the way for her promotion to team leader. Their experiences are shared by thousands of other Thai students who have benefited from the Luban Workshop. Named after an ancient Chinese craftsman, the workshop embodies China's tradition of craftsmanship and innovation while equipping Thai youth with practical skills. In March 2016, Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College in China and Ayutthaya Technical College jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop in Thailand. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system. A student builds an installation system of automation production line at the Luban Workshop of Ayutthaya Technical College in Ayutthaya, Thailand, March 14, 2023. (Xinhua/Wang Teng) Recalling the workshop's early days, Jarun Youbrum, then director of Ayutthaya Technical College who was involved throughout its establishment, expressed deep appreciation for the Chinese instructors. "To help assemble and commission the equipment, they would sometimes work until two in the morning," Jarun said. "Their dedication is truly moving." Following three phases of development, the workshop's instructional space has expanded 10 folds to 2,000 square meters, with 15 teaching and practice areas established. According to Pakorn Muangsuk, head of the college's Mechatronics and Robotics department, Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College has regularly sent instructors to Thailand to train students. Ayutthaya Technical College has also dispatched its faculty to China to learn equipment operation and teaching methods. Pakorn's department adopted the EPIP (Engineering Practice Innovation Project) teaching model, which helps students build professional knowledge and practical skills through real-world engineering projects and targeted problem-solving. One valuable opportunity offered by the workshop is further training in Tianjin. Teerapat Sudso, an Internet of Things (IoT) major who enrolled in 2018, was selected to study there for over a year. Teerapat has now been working for over three years as an assistant engineer at the Thai subsidiary of Zhongji Innolight, a leading Chinese manufacturer of high-speed optical modules. He mentors both Chinese and Thai apprentices. Teerapat said the knowledge and skills he acquired at the workshop laid the foundation for his current role, and he still uses Chinese at work every day. "Graduates from our college possess both professional skills and the ability to communicate in Chinese, which gives them a distinct advantage when seeking employment," said Pakorn. He added that as Chinese-funded enterprises continue to establish factories and begin production in Ayutthaya's industrial parks, demand for frontline workers is steadily growing. Chaowarit Umboon, deputy director of Ayutthaya Technical College, speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Ayutthaya, Thailand, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Sun Weitong) Statistics from Ayutthaya Technical College show that over the past decade, Luban Workshop has cultivated more than 2,600 local students pursuing academic degrees and sent over 500 students to China for further study. Meanwhile, the Chinese and Thai colleges have jointly trained nearly 100,000 people through their partnership. A new milestone was reached in September, when Ayutthaya Technical College inaugurated the world's first EPIP Center, jointly established with Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College. The center features practical training modules in artificial intelligence, IoT, intelligent manufacturing, and other fields. "Luban Workshop has established a cooperation network spanning multiple vocational colleges, providing students from these institutions with opportunities to study in China," said Chaowarit Umboon, deputy director of Ayutthaya Technical College. Looking ahead, Chaowarit hopes to see more branch centers established across northern, southern, and northeastern Thailand, making it easier for students in these regions to pursue further studies and receive practical training. item.title: APEC comes to Shenzhen: where "China Opportunity 2.0" meets the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Explainer: APEC comes to Shenzhen: where "China Opportunity 2.0" meets the world This photo taken on Nov. 13, 2026 shows a view of Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Next week, the gaze of the Asia-Pacific will turn to a young metropolis in southern China that, about four decades ago, was little more than a quiet fishing village. Shenzhen will play host to the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting -- the first time in 12 years that China has hosted the top event of the region's highest-level, most extensive and most influential economic cooperation mechanism. China officially joined APEC in 1991. Shenzhen, adjacent to Hong Kong, will become the third Chinese city after Shanghai and Beijing to welcome this gathering. Its rise over the past few decades stands as a miracle in the annals of global development, demonstrating what the Chinese people can achieve. When Shenzhen was designated a special economic zone in 1980, its GDP stood at just 270 million yuan (around 40.2 million U.S. dollars). By 2025, that figure had soared to 3.87 trillion yuan, trailing only Shanghai and Beijing. China's choice of Shenzhen mirrors a pattern common to other APEC economies, which tend to favor national capitals, major economic or technological hubs, or internationally renowned tourist destinations as host cities. For the 2026 APEC "China Year," China has set openness, innovation and cooperation as its three priorities. They echo the very forces that have shaped Shenzhen's development: openness is the city's defining feature, innovation its greatest strength, and cooperation a driving force behind its continued growth. An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 20, 2026 shows a cargo ship sailing toward Yantian Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua) MARKET FOR THE WORLD Shenzhen's rise over more than forty years owes much to China's reform and opening up. One of the country's first special economic zones, Shenzhen has been a city of opportunity from the very beginning, pioneering one move after another. Countless entrepreneurs and innovators have gone there to pursue their ambitions, international investors have established a presence, and Chinese companies such as BYD and Huawei have grown from local businesses into global players. Shenzhen's tale has unfolded in step with the country's opening up. Today, China is expanding high-standard opening up. It has granted zero-tariff treatment to 63 countries, while remaining the world's second-largest importer for 17 consecutive years. In recent years, alongside further opening up the flow of goods, services, capital and talent, China has steadily expanded institutional opening up -- a key hallmark of high-standard opening up -- with respect to rules, regulations, management, and standards. The aim is to build a business environment that is transparent, stable and predictable, and to bring China's institutional framework into closer alignment with international standards. Shenzhen is a core city in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Under "one country, two systems," the area's distinctive environment of three customs territories and three currencies has created valuable opportunities to explore the alignment of legal rules, cross-border professional practice, mutual recognition of qualifications, streamlined customs clearance and common standards. In this sense, the area serves as a testing ground for bridging different systems and improving institutional connectivity across the Asia-Pacific. This photo taken on Nov. 11, 2026 shows a coffee service area at the media center for the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian) INNOVATION DIVIDENDS Today's Shenzhen is internationally known for its technological prowess and is often dubbed "China's Silicon Valley." It now boasts more than 2 million professionals in science and technology. Yet when the special economic zone was first established in 1980, the city's entire pool of technical personnel consisted of just two people: a tractor mechanic and a veterinarian. This contrast captures the scale of Shenzhen's transformation. In recent years, Shenzhen's output of new energy vehicles, industrial robots and civilian drones has maintained double-digit growth for extended periods. The city has also become a popular destination for shoppers and technology enthusiasts looking to scour Huaqiangbei, its famed electronics market, for the latest products and cutting-edge innovations. China's industrial strengths in emerging sectors such as renewable energy and electric vehicles are no accident. They are the result of years of technological accumulation, well-developed industrial supply chains, and the opportunities created by a vast domestic market. If the "China Opportunity 1.0" of the past was largely about offering the world market dividends via China's enormous consumer market and low-cost production factors, today's "China Opportunity 2.0" is about delivering even greater market dividends while generating innovation dividends through technological progress and industrial upgrading. In China, businesses from around the world can quickly find partners to work with across the entire process, from research and development and prototype testing to mass production. Companies can tap into the Chinese market while strengthening their competitiveness in global markets. Seeing these advantages, foreign companies have increasingly moved beyond simply selling their products in China in recent years. Many have also established research and development centers and regional headquarters in the country. In 2025, 14,000 new foreign-invested enterprises were established in China's scientific research and technical services sector, a year-on-year increase of 27.2 percent. This photo taken on Nov. 3, 2026 shows a view of Shennan Avenue in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) COOPERATION FOR SHARED PROSPERITY The ocean connects rather than divides. Linked by the Pacific, the Asia-Pacific is one of the world's most dynamic economic regions, with deeply integrated regional economies and closely interconnected industrial and supply chains. Cooperation underpins the shared prosperity of the Asia-Pacific and is essential to building an Asia-Pacific community. Against a backdrop of rising unilateralism and protectionism, one of China's most important responsibilities as APEC host is to help bring economies back to the path of openness and cooperation. With global challenges -- climate change, food and energy security, demographic shifts and development imbalances -- intertwined and compounding, no single economy can prosper alone. Over the past year, the 2026 APEC "China Year" has produced substantial results. Working with other APEC member economies, China has organized more than 300 APEC meetings and events, which covered a wide range of areas, including trade, tourism, small and medium-sized enterprises, and energy. They helped build consensus on a series of areas for cooperation. Next week in Shenzhen, participating economies are expected to build on that consensus and deliver more practical outcomes in key areas such as trade, connectivity, the digital economy and artificial intelligence. Such progress would provide fresh impetus for economic growth and prosperity across the Asia-Pacific and beyond. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Shenzhen opens its doors wider to the Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Shenzhen opens its doors wider to the Asia-Pacific Shenzhen, a coastal city in south China's Guangdong Province, will host the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19. Shenzhen has grown from a fishing village into an international metropolis and much of that came from openness and cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region. Now the city is giving back, contributing to the region's development with renewed confidence. Chinese President Xi Jinping extended an invitation to the world at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Gyeongju, South Korea, last November. "We look forward to all parties gathering in Shenzhen next year to jointly discuss development plans for the Asia-Pacific region and create a bright future for it," Xi said. As a window into China's reform and opening up, Shenzhen offers the world a glimpse of a more open and inclusive China. Visitors pose for photos with an APEC-themed display at Lianhuashan Park in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Visitors from around the world are flocking to Huaqiangbei, known as "China's No. 1 Electronics Street," to shop for products such as AI glasses, drones and 3D printers. Goods from the street now reach more than 190 countries and regions. The hub receives an average of more than 7,000 foreign visitors a day, and its annual sales exceed 400 billion yuan (about $60 billion). A similar scene is playing out in the robot block of Shenzhen's Longgang district. "In Shenzhen, I saw a picture of the future," said Emaunel Cardoso, a South American buyer shopping for a robot dog. He hopes to work with Chinese firms on materials and machinery. Visa-free policies, including 240-hour visa-free transit, have boosted international travel to the city. The number of foreign nationals entering and leaving China through Shenzhen ranked second nationwide in 2025. Meanwhile, Shenzhen's ports handled 273 million passenger trips, the highest figure in the country. APEC-themed flags hang on the robot block in Longgang district, Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Cargo is moving faster too. At Shenzhen airport's international cargo center, customs offers advance declaration and round-the-clock clearance by appointment for time-sensitive imports. So far this year, Shenzhen Airport Customs has cleared 8,500 tonnes of fresh produce and live seafood from APEC economies, including durians from Malaysia and wax apples from Thailand. The surge in travelers and cargo underscores the growing confidence of global investors in Shenzhen's business environment. As the global landscape shifts, Asia-Pacific economies are further opening their markets and building stronger consensus on win-win development. At the world's first robot 6S store in Shenzhen, a Malaysian businesswoman's smart coffee machines are popular among consumers. Drawn by China's incentives for foreign investment, she set up business in Shenzhen. Strong sales of her smart office products highlight the appeal of the Chinese market, and several Asia-Pacific firms have established operations in the city since the start of this year. Chinese companies are expanding overseas as well. The Longgang Enterprise Internationalization Service Base has served 9,494 companies looking to grow abroad, releasing orders worth more than 13.5 billion yuan (about $1.9 billion) and facilitating intent agreements worth a further 1 billion yuan, according to Li Qun, deputy general manager of Shenzhen Longgang Industrial Investment Service Group Co., Ltd. Photo shows APEC-themed displays on Shennan Avenue in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) China's trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent year on year to 24.07 trillion yuan in the first three quarters of 2026. As of 2025, China had become the largest trading partner of 13 APEC economies. During the 2026 APEC "China Year," some 300 events are expected to take place across multiple cities in China, underscoring the country's commitment to multilateralism and regional economic integration. Across the Asia-Pacific, the benefits of greater openness are spreading further and faster. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is now in force for all 15 members, with tariffs on more than 90 percent of goods traded within the region due to be eliminated over the coming decades. The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol was signed in October 2025. Openness is a sure path for Asia-Pacific countries to achieve common prosperity. Amid global turbulence, only by expanding opening up and deepening cooperation can regional economies provide greater certainty and create new opportunities for the Asia-Pacific and the world. "Only by working together can Asia-Pacific countries, like passengers on the same boat, sail toward a better future," said Rinaldo Hartanto, a young Indonesian artist working in Shenzhen.
